 A pedestrian crosses West King Street in this photo, taken at 8:10 a.m. on Jan. 7, 1974. Many people who worked in the city of Lancaster were going to work in the dark, thanks to an experiment in year-round Daylight Saving Time.
 Daylight saving time ends this Sunday, meaning it'll once again be time to turn the clocks back one hour.
 But did you know the United States has tried to keep daylight saving time year-round? And, Lancaster County residents weren't exactly thrilled about it.
 The federal government began an experiment with permanent daylight saving time in January 1974 amid a national energy crisis. The idea was to ultimately reduce energy consumption in exchange for darker mornings.
 Lancaster County residents didn't hesitate to voice their frustrations. County school districts adjusted their schedules, students had to wait for their buses in the dark and some city workers didn't feel safe walking to work in the dark.
 Ultimately, the experiment was unpopular, with Congress restoring standard time later that same year. 
 History 
 We tried year-round Daylight Saving Time in 1974 and people in Lancaster County hated it [Archives]

 More than 50 years later, efforts to make daylight saving time permanent are once again moving through Congress.
 The U.S. House of Representatives passed the Sunshine Protection Act of 2025 on July 14. The bill would once again make permanent daylight saving time the national standard, but preserves standard time options for states that are exempt from it (like Hawaii and Arizona). The bill is currently awaiting further action in the Senate.
 A 2025 poll from The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research shows that if forced to choose, most Americans would prefer to keep that extra hour of daylight in the evening. Only 12% of U.S. adults favor the current system of daylight saving time, which requires people in most states to change their clocks twice a year, while 47% oppose it and 40% are neutral.
 And if forced to choose between permanent daylight saving time and permanent standard time, 56% of Americans would prefer to keep that extra hour of daylight in the evening.
 For now, clocks will still turn back one hour at 2 a.m. Sunday, Nov. 1.
 The Associated Press contributed to this report.
